questions.stem: All glucose is normally reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule. A patient with uncontrolled diabetes has glucose in their urine. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The patient's kidneys have stopped filtering glucose
Blood glucose levels are so high that the transport proteins in the tubule become saturated and cannot reabsorb all the glucose
The patient is drinking too much water, diluting the glucose
Glucose is being actively secreted into the tubule by kidney cells

questions.explanation: Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport using specific carrier proteins. In uncontrolled diabetes, blood glucose is extremely high, so the filtrate contains more glucose than the transport proteins can handle. The excess glucose remains in the tubule and appears in the urine.

questions.stem: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria and microvilli. How do these features relate to their function in selective reabsorption?

options.text: Mitochondria produce glucose; microvilli store water
Mitochondria provide ATP for active transport; microvilli increase surface area for reabsorption
Mitochondria increase surface area; microvilli produce ATP
Both features help with ultrafiltration, not reabsorption

questions.explanation: Many substances are reabsorbed by active transport, which requires ATP — hence the abundant mitochondria. The microvilli greatly increase the surface area of the tubule lining, allowing more efficient reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, and ions from the filtrate.

questions.stem: A scientist compares the composition of filtrate at the start and end of the proximal convoluted tubule. Which change would they observe?

options.text: Glucose concentration increases; urea concentration decreases
All glucose and most amino acids have been reabsorbed; urea remains in the filtrate
Urea has been completely reabsorbed; glucose remains
The composition is unchanged because reabsorption occurs in the loop of Henle

questions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs all glucose, all amino acids, and much of the water and ions back into the blood. Urea is not actively reabsorbed here (it is a waste product), so it remains in the filtrate to be excreted in urine.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the sodium-potassium pumps in the kidney tubule cells. What effect would this have on selective reabsorption?

options.text: Reabsorption of glucose and amino acids would increase
Reabsorption of glucose and amino acids would decrease because active transport depends on the sodium gradient these pumps create
Only water reabsorption would be affected
There would be no effect because reabsorption is entirely passive

questions.explanation: Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed via co-transport with sodium ions, which depends on the sodium concentration gradient created by sodium-potassium pumps. Blocking these pumps would disrupt the gradient, reducing reabsorption and causing these substances to be lost in urine.

questions.stem: Approximately 180 litres of filtrate are produced per day, but only about 1.5 litres of urine are excreted. What does this tell us about the efficiency of selective reabsorption?

options.text: The kidneys are failing to filter blood properly
Over 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed back into the blood, showing highly efficient selective reabsorption
Most of the filtrate evaporates before reaching the bladder
The body produces 178.5 litres of sweat per day to compensate

questions.explanation: The huge difference between filtrate volume (180 L) and urine volume (1.5 L) shows that over 99% of the filtrate — including nearly all water, glucose, and useful substances — is selectively reabsorbed back into the blood. Only waste products and excess water are excreted.
